claims.text: Wear resistance in HEA protective coatings is governed primarily by load-induced dynamic amorphization.
Load-induced transformation refines a coarse initial grain structure into an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer.
The ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior.
Inverse Hall-Petch behavior lowers shear strength as grain size is reduced.
The refined near-surface layer lowers friction and improves wear resistance.
CoCrFeMnNi is a single-phase HEA relevant to the proposed initial state.
The proposed HEA coatings initially have a coarse-grained microstructure.
Controlled sliding deformation under inert or ultra-high-vacuum conditions can induce dynamic amorphization at the surface.
Ultra-high-vacuum or inert testing mitigates oxidation and formation of mixed metal-oxide films.
Systematic variation of load and sliding speed can trigger a transition from coarse grains to an ultra-nanocrystalline surface state.
The mechanically transformed samples will develop a near-surface nanocrystalline structure detectable by STEM.
The transformed material will exhibit a friction coefficient of approximately 0.3.
The transformed material will exhibit a wear rate of approximately 10^-6 mm^3/(N·m).
Coarse-grained baseline samples that do not effectively form the nanocrystalline layer will have higher friction and wear rates than transformed samples.
The proposed behavior holds across a range of mechanical loads and sliding speeds in inert or ultra-high-vacuum environments.
Oxidation or HEA composition changes may significantly alter the dynamic amorphization process.
Failure to form an ultra-nanocrystalline layer or failure to reduce friction and wear relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
